headline: Your iPhone Is Missing AI in Europe, and It's Only Going to Get More Complicated
headline_options: Your iPhone Is Missing AI in Europe, and It's Only Going to Get More Complicated
selected_headline: Your iPhone Is Missing AI in Europe, and It's Only Going to Get More Complicated
body_markdown:
If you own an iPhone in France, Germany, or anywhere else in the European Union, you will not get the new Siri AI when iOS 27 ships this fall. Not because [Apple](https://www.apple.com) couldn't build it. Because regulators said no. That single fact is the clearest window into a much bigger story: Europe's **Digital Markets Act** has turned your smartphone into a geopolitical chess piece, and the endgame is about who controls the AI layer on every device you own.

## What the Digital Markets Act Actually Does

The **DMA**, which took full effect in 2023, is the European Union's attempt to stop a small group of tech platforms from locking competitors out of the digital economy. It designates certain companies as **"gatekeepers"** — platforms so dominant that their control over key infrastructure gives them an unfair structural advantage. Once you earn that label, you face a specific set of obligations: you must allow interoperability, you cannot favor your own services, and you must give rivals meaningful access to the systems users depend on.

Apple is a gatekeeper for iOS, iPadOS, and the App Store. [Google](https://www.google.com) is a gatekeeper for Android. Both companies have fought the designation, and both have lost. On July 8, 2026, the EU General Court rejected Apple's legal challenge to its gatekeeper status outright, leaving the company with no procedural escape hatch.

Fines for non-compliance are not symbolic. The DMA allows penalties of up to **10 percent of a company's global annual turnover**, which in Apple's case would run into the tens of billions of dollars.

## Why Apple Is Blocking Siri AI in the EU

Apple's position is not that it refuses to comply. It's that the EU has rejected every compliance proposal Apple has submitted. Apple SVP Craig Federighi said it plainly in June 2026: the European Commission's unwillingness to engage on solutions that protect privacy and security means there is currently no set timeline for Siri AI on iOS or iPadOS in the EU.

The core tension is about **deep OS access**. The EU's interoperability rules require that if Siri AI can read your notifications, control your smart home, or pull context from third-party apps, then rival AI assistants must be able to do the same things at the same system level. Apple argues that granting that kind of access to any third-party AI creates security vulnerabilities and privacy risks that its architecture was never designed to absorb.

The EU's counter-position is essentially: that's a convenient excuse to keep competitors out. Both sides have a point, which is exactly why the standoff has no clean resolution. Apple CEO Tim Cook and EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen held a virtual meeting in late June 2026 that both sides described as "constructive." No timeline emerged from it.

For now, **450 million iPhone and iPad users** across the EU will open iOS 27 this fall and find a version of Siri that stops well short of what users in the US, UK, Switzerland, and Norway will experience. Notably, Siri AI will still function on Mac and Vision Pro in the EU, since those devices fall under different gatekeeper classifications.

[IMAGE #IMG2: Tim Cook on a video call, viewed from behind a laptop screen showing a blurred EU flag backdrop, natural office lighting, candid editorial moment]

## How Google Ended Up in a Different Position

Google's situation with Android looks similar on the surface but plays out very differently in practice. The EU is preparing a final ruling on Android AI access rules, with a decision deadline of July 27, 2026. That ruling would require Google to grant third-party AI assistants the same system-level access that its own **Gemini** assistant receives.

On paper, this is a significant demand. Google has spent years building Gemini into Android's core functions, and opening those hooks to competitors is not a trivial engineering ask. But here is the key difference from Apple's situation: Android's architecture, as an open-source platform, already has more permeable boundaries than iOS. Google has more room to demonstrate compliance without fundamentally restructuring how its OS works.

There is also a strategic calculation at play. The Verge's reporting on this dynamic notes that Google has become considerably better at navigating EU regulatory processes than Apple. Accepting a structured obligation, even a costly one, is preferable to the reputational and financial damage of a prolonged standoff. Google knows how to negotiate the shape of a rule. Apple, culturally, finds it harder to accept that a regulator gets to define what happens inside its operating system.

What makes this moment stranger still: Apple has publicly backed Google's criticism of the proposed Android AI rules, warning in a May 2026 submission to the European Commission that forcing open AI access could "undermine privacy, weaken security, and impact how devices perform." Two fierce competitors, aligned against the same regulator.

[IMAGE #IMG3: Side-by-side of an iPhone and an Android phone on a flat surface, both showing their respective AI assistant screens, shot from directly above, clean neutral background]

## Who This Actually Affects and What Comes Next

The immediate losers are EU consumers who will use less capable AI features than their counterparts elsewhere, at least temporarily. But the longer-term implications run deeper than a delayed software feature.

If the EU succeeds in forcing genuine AI interoperability on both platforms, it creates a world where a European user could set a third-party AI assistant, from a startup, a local provider, or a rival tech giant, as their default and have it work at the same depth as the built-in option. That is a meaningful shift in market structure, not just a policy footnote.

The EU is simultaneously investigating Apple, Google, and [Meta](https://www.meta.com) for five separate potential DMA breaches, covering issues from anti-steering rules to search bias. Those investigations are expected to run roughly 12 months. The July 27 Android ruling will be the next concrete signal of how aggressively the Commission intends to push.

Europe is not just regulating apps. It is trying to determine who gets to own the AI layer of everyday computing. Whether that produces genuine competition or just compliance theater depends entirely on enforcement details that are still being written.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is Siri AI blocked in the EU but not in the UK?

The UK left the European Union and is not subject to the Digital Markets Act. The DMA's gatekeeper rules apply only within EU member states, which is why users in the UK, Switzerland, and Norway will receive Siri AI with iOS 27 while EU users will not. Apple's block is specifically a response to unresolved DMA compliance negotiations, not a global product decision.

### What exactly is a DMA "gatekeeper" and does it only apply to Apple and Google?

A gatekeeper is a platform the European Commission designates as a critical digital gateway, one with durable market power that competitors must pass through to reach users. As of mid-2026, designated gatekeepers include Apple (for iOS, iPadOS, and the App Store), Google (for Android, Google Search, and Google Maps), Meta (for Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp), and others. Each gatekeeper faces tailored obligations based on which services earned the designation.

### Could Apple face fines for withholding Siri AI in the EU?

The DMA's penalty structure allows fines up to 10 percent of global annual turnover for non-compliance, and up to 20 percent for repeat violations. However, Apple's current position is that it cannot comply because the EU has rejected its proposals, not that it is refusing to comply. Whether the Commission treats that distinction as a valid defense or as a stalling tactic is the central legal question. Active investigations into Apple already cover five separate potential breaches.

### Will third-party AI assistants ever be able to replace Siri or Gemini at a system level?

That is precisely what the EU's interoperability push is designed to enable. If the Android AI access rules finalized on July 27, 2026 hold, and if Apple eventually reaches a DMA agreement, users in the EU could theoretically set a third-party assistant as their device default with equivalent access to system functions. In practice, the depth of that access will depend on how broadly "equal access" gets defined and enforced, and that negotiation is still actively in progress.
